prompt.context: Our client is the head of the R&D department of a pharmaceutical company. He wants us to advise him on how to improve the productivity in the R&D department. There are basically several steps leading from the discovery of the molecule to the launch: Discovery (discovery of the molecule), Preclinical (testing on animals), Phase 1 (testing on humans), Phase 2 (testing on humans), Phase 3 (testing on humans), and Approval & Launch. It normally takes about 10 years to discover a drug and get it approved. The drugs are usually patent protected.
prompt.question: How would you improve the productivity of the R&D department? If you had to measure R&D productivity in terms of a formula you could present to shareholders, what would that formula be, and what are the key drivers to increase it?

clarifying_info.q: What specific stage of the pipeline is the client most concerned about?
clarifying_info.a: The client is concerned about overall R&D productivity across all stages.

clarifying_info.q: Are there specific cost or time constraints we should be aware of?
clarifying_info.a: The drugs take about 10 years to discover and get approved; patent protection makes the length of research a key driver of returns.

framework: Define a measurable productivity formula: (NPV of future cashflows of successful drugs minus R&D cost of all drugs) divided by R&D cost of all drugs
Analyze drivers of NPV of future cashflows from successful drugs: quality of compound, length of research cycle, marketing & sales effectiveness
Analyze drivers of R&D cost across all drugs: stage-gate discipline, quality of scientists, build-vs-buy decisions for compounds
Assess R&D organizational factors: scientist motivation and retention, incentive structure design
Synthesize into a prioritized set of recommendations

questions.prompt: How would you measure R&D productivity in a formula presentable to shareholders?
questions.guidance: A strong answer frames productivity as value created per dollar invested. The candidate should arrive at: (NPV of future cashflows of successful drugs - R&D cost of all drugs) / R&D cost of all drugs. This captures both the revenue upside and the cost denominator in a single ratio.

math.setup: Productivity = (NPV of future cashflows of successful drugs - R&D cost of all drugs) / R&D cost of all drugs
steps: Numerator: NPV of cashflows from drugs that successfully reach market, minus total R&D spend on all drugs (including failures)
Denominator: Total R&D investment across all drug candidates
Result expresses return per dollar of R&D invested
math.answer: Productivity ratio = (NPV of successful drug cashflows - Total R&D cost) / Total R&D cost

questions.prompt: What are the big drivers to increase R&D productivity on the revenue/NPV side?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through each component of the NPV numerator: (1) Quality of the compound — highest-quality compounds generate sustained revenues (e.g., Lipitor). Sufficient testing during trial phases prevents side effects that destroy commercial value. (2) Length of research — reducing the 10-year cycle extends effective patent life and maximizes time-to-revenue. (3) Marketing & Sales — while outside the R&D head's direct control, awareness and demand-building by the commercial team directly affects realized cashflows.

questions.prompt: What are the big drivers to reduce R&D cost across all drugs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) Strict stage-gate controls — no drug with a high likelihood of failing should advance to the next stage. Early failure avoidance prevents wasted spend on later (more expensive) patient testing. (2) Quality scientists — high-caliber talent improves both the probability of success and the efficiency of research. (3) Acquire or partner on externally developed compounds — buying compounds that have already passed early stages diversifies risk and avoids duplicating costly early-stage work in-house.

questions.prompt: What other organizational factors affect R&D productivity?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise scientist motivation and retention. The R&D cycle is ~10 years, so scientists may leave before seeing their drug succeed. Retaining critical talent is essential because knowledge loss mid-cycle is extremely costly.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest challenge the R&D head faces today?
questions.guidance: Evaluating scientist teams: defining measurable, fair metrics and assessing performance against them is the core management challenge in a long-cycle, high-uncertainty environment.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest mistake an R&D head could make when designing scientist incentives?
questions.guidance: Measuring scientists on the number of drugs passed from one stage to the next. This creates perverse incentives to advance borderline or unsuitable drugs, dramatically increasing R&D costs and wasting time that could be spent on more promising candidates. The correct incentive structure should be compliance-based: rewarding adherence to stage-gate guidelines, and holding scientists accountable when a drug fails at a later stage due to a lapse in a prior stage they controlled.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the ways an R&D head could improve productivity?

categories.name: Pipeline / Stage-Gate Discipline
ideas: Implement strict go/no-go criteria at each development stage
Use predictive biomarkers and diagnostics to terminate failing compounds earlier
Conduct regular portfolio reviews to kill low-probability projects
Standardize decision criteria across therapeutic areas

categories.name: Research Efficiency
ideas: Invest in platform technologies that accelerate discovery (e.g., high-throughput screening, AI-assisted molecule design)
Reduce cycle time at each phase through parallel trial designs
Use adaptive trial designs to shorten Phase 2/3 timelines
Outsource non-core research activities to CROs

categories.name: External Innovation
ideas: Acquire or in-license compounds that have cleared early stages
Form partnerships with biotech firms for co-development
Establish open-innovation programs with academia
Pursue co-development deals to share risk and cost

categories.name: Talent & Organization
ideas: Design compliance-based incentive structures (not stage-count based)
Build retention programs for key scientists given the 10-year cycle
Create cross-functional teams to reduce handoff friction
Establish mentorship and career pathways to reduce attrition

categories.name: Resource Allocation
ideas: Concentrate investment in highest-probability compounds
Use portfolio modeling to balance risk across therapeutic areas
Benchmark R&D spend against industry peers
Automate low-value administrative tasks to free scientist time

recommendation: Shorten the length of the research cycle so that successful drugs achieve maximum remaining patent life, maximizing NPV of future cashflows
Establish strict stage-gate guidelines at each phase to identify and eliminate failing compounds as early as possible, reducing wasted R&D investment
Redesign scientist incentive structures to be compliance-driven rather than based on the number of drugs advanced, eliminating the incentive to push borderline compounds forward
risks: Over-tightening stage-gate criteria could kill viable compounds too early, reducing the pipeline
Compliance-based incentives may be difficult to define objectively across diverse drug types
External acquisition of compounds introduces integration and IP risk
next_steps: Audit current stage-gate criteria and compare pass rates to industry benchmarks
Review existing scientist performance metrics and redesign with compliance focus
Identify external partnership or acquisition targets for compounds in Phase 1-2
